strengths: Soundness: The paper identifies a real optimization problem in mid-stage width expansion and provides an intuitive decomposition into signal preservation and symmetry breaking. The symmetry-lock argument correctly captures why duplicated channels with symmetric optimizer states remain redundant, even though some displayed gradient equations omit common scaling factors.

Evidence: The ablations are unusually extensive in initialization space: Figures 1–5 examine multiple fan-in/fan-out initialization pairs, hidden and expert-intermediate expansion, optimizer-state handling, and learning-rate re-warmup. Appendices G–H add Muon and comparisons with perturbation, uneven splitting, and global re-warmup.

Significance: If validated more rigorously, 20–35% estimated FLOP savings and 1.27–1.49× measured wall-clock speedups at comparable token budgets would be practically useful for expensive MoE pre-training.

Originality: Combining RMS-aware rescaling with asymmetric optimizer-state retention and parameter-selective re-warmup is a useful perspective on mid-training width growth. The focus on balancing forward continuity against backward symmetry is clearer than treating expansion as initialization alone.
Presentation: The manuscript is generally well organized, visually polished, and includes derivations, model/training configurations, computational-cost measurements, and component-wise ablations.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claim that RMS preservation is the mechanism underlying successful expansion is stronger than the evidence. The derivation assumes centered, independent, homoscedastic fan-in terms and isotropic activations, assumptions that are not established for trained Transformers. Direct activation evidence is limited largely to aggregate MLP RMS ratios in Figure 4; there is no layerwise distributional analysis or causal comparison against alternative statistic-preserving criteria.

The both-sides-copy rule for copy ratio c>1 is not generally valid as written. Equation 37 assumes every original coordinate has multiplicity 1+c, whereas the text only says that some dimensions may be copied multiple times. In general, variance depends on the sum of squared per-coordinate multiplicities, so no scaling factor determined solely by c exists without specifying the copy allocation. Equations 20 and 40 also omit expansion scaling factors, even though this omission does not change the equality-of-gradients conclusion.

Evaluation uncertainty is not reported. All curves and downstream scores appear to come from single runs, with no seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The claimed downstream advantage over from-scratch training is therefore unconvincing, especially because SPARKLING retains worse pre-training loss in every setting and much of its average-score gain is driven by the Arithmetic benchmark.

The baseline comparison is confounded and internally unclear. From-scratch target models use size-specific step-law learning rates, whereas expanded models retain the smaller model's peak rate; Table 4 reports 1.9556e-3 while Table 5 reports 1.449e-3 for the baseline. This discrepancy and the substantially different post-expansion learning-rate treatment make it difficult to know whether gains arise from expansion, better tuning, or the proposed mechanism. Compute-matched quality curves and separately tuned baselines are needed.

Generality is overstated. The empirical study uses one OLMoE-style architecture and one expansion time (100B of 200B tokens), at no more than 1.5B active parameters. Muon is tested only for expert-inner expansion, apparently without full downstream evaluation. There is no dense-model experiment, alternative architecture, different expansion ratio, or sweep over early/mid/late expansion times.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite listing several hyperparameters. The manuscript does not specify the training corpus and mixture, tokenizer/data processing, evaluation harness and shot/prompt settings, random seeds, exact architecture-expansion mapping, or implementation of optimizer-state slicing and separate learning rates within enlarged tensors. No code or complete algorithm is provided.

The limitations section is too narrow: it mentions only future depth expansion and µP compatibility, but not the single architecture, modest scale, single expansion point, lack of repeated trials, theoretical assumptions, or baseline-tuning ambiguity. There is also no explicit research-ethics discussion covering data provenance, benchmark contamination, licensing, or the environmental implications of the reported 64-A100 experiments.

Overall, the paper contains a promising and potentially useful method, but unsupported general claims, baseline ambiguity, lack of uncertainty estimates, and insufficient reproducibility prevent reliable acceptance in its current form. A revised evaluation with repeated runs, compute-matched and tuned controls, precise data/evaluation disclosure, and broader expansion settings could materially change the recommendation.

strengths: Significance: The manuscript addresses mid-stage width expansion, a practically relevant and comparatively underexplored route to reducing language-model pretraining cost. The reported 20–35% FLOP savings and 1.27–1.49× wall-clock speedups would be useful if the performance claims were established robustly. Soundness: The paper develops an intuitively coherent recipe combining RMS-aware rescaling, asymmetric optimizer-state reset, and asymmetric learning-rate re-warmup. Its experiments cover expert-inner, hidden-dimension, and joint expansion, as well as AdamW and Muon.

Presentation: The motivating distinction between forward signal preservation and backward symmetry breaking is clear. The progression from initialization studies to optimizer-state and learning-rate ablations is easy to follow, and the figures are legible.

Originality: Treating mid-stage width growth through the joint lens of RMS preservation and optimization asymmetry provides a useful synthesis, even though the individual mechanisms are relatively simple and closely related to prior variance-transfer, symmetry-breaking, and learning-rate adaptation techniques.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central empirical claims appear to rely on single runs. No seeds, confidence intervals, or variance estimates are reported for either pretraining loss or downstream accuracy. Many highlighted loss differences are extremely small, while the downstream averages combine noisy tasks and differ by roughly 0.5–1.7 points. The evidence therefore does not establish that SPARKLING reliably outperforms from-scratch training.

Soundness: The comparison to from-scratch models is confounded by learning-rate selection. Appendix B states that from-scratch target models use size-specific step-law learning rates, whereas expanded models retain the small model’s peak rate. Table 4 reports a 1.9556e-3 peak rate that also disagrees with the 1.449e-3 baseline rate in Table 5. Without controlled tuning for every baseline, superiority cannot confidently be attributed to the proposed expansion method.

Soundness: The paper does not include a compute-matched baseline, such as training the target-width model from scratch for fewer tokens at the same FLOP or wall-clock budget. Comparing at an equal 200B-token budget demonstrates arithmetic savings but does not show that progressive expansion is the best use of the saved compute.

Soundness: The RMS derivation is much less general than the prose suggests. It assumes centered, homoscedastic, mutually independent weights and activations—conditions that are unlikely to hold in a trained Transformer. The RMSNorm derivation substitutes parameter variance for its second moment despite scale parameters generally having nonzero mean. Moreover, the c>1 copy formula assumes uniform duplication multiplicity, although the text allows only some dimensions to be copied repeatedly; in that setting the variance depends on the sum of squared multiplicities. Thus the claimed systematic preservation principle is partly heuristic and is only tested at 2× growth.

Soundness: The proposed causal explanations are not directly validated. The paper does not report layerwise RMS errors across the principal experiments, nor measurements of copied-neuron similarity, effective rank, or feature diversification. Better loss after asymmetric reset or re-warmup is compatible with generic optimization benefits and does not by itself demonstrate that a symmetry lock was the operative bottleneck.

Evaluation scope: All large-scale evidence uses variants of one OLMoE-style architecture, one 50% expansion point, one token budget, and primarily one dataset/training recipe. The Muon study covers only expert-inner expansion. This is insufficient support for broad claims of generality across model families, optimizers, expansion timing, and width axes.

Presentation and reproducibility: Essential details are missing, including the pretraining data mixture and preprocessing, tokenizer provenance, evaluation prompts/few-shot settings and harness, random seeds, precise channel-copy mappings, router treatment, and implementation/code availability. The unusual decoupling of hidden size from attention dimensions also needs a complete specification. Others could not reliably reproduce the reported results from the manuscript alone.

Limitations and ethics: The conclusion lists future extensions but does not candidly discuss the study’s principal limitations, statistical uncertainty, baseline sensitivity, or narrow architectural scope. There is also no treatment of dataset provenance, benchmark contamination, energy cost, or broader risks associated with the trained language models. These omissions are especially notable given the 64×A100, 200B-token experiments.

Overall: The problem is worthwhile and the recipe is promising, but unsupported robustness claims, confounded baselines, limited validation of the proposed mechanisms, and inadequate reproducibility prevent acceptance in its current form. Multiple controlled repetitions, compute-matched and equally tuned baselines, direct mechanism measurements, and fuller implementation details are needed.

strengths: Soundness: The empirical story is coherent and unusually well ablated. The manuscript tests five initialization pairs, expert-intermediate and hidden-size expansion, asymmetric optimizer-state handling, learning-rate re-warmup, and both AdamW and Muon. The resulting loss curves consistently support the proposed preservation/symmetry trade-off.

Significance: Mid-training width expansion addresses a practically important but understudied source of pre-training savings. At a fixed 200B-token budget, the reported 20–35% FLOP savings and 1.27–1.49× wall-clock speedups are meaningful, while SPARKLING attains higher average downstream accuracy than the corresponding from-scratch models in all three expansion settings.

Originality: Framing width growth as jointly requiring activation-scale preservation and backward-symmetry breaking is insightful. In particular, preserving the copied forward computation while breaking symmetry through asymmetric optimizer states and parameter-specific re-warmup is a simple, useful design.

Presentation: The paper is well organized and visually polished. Its progression from the RMS analysis to symmetry lock, interventions, ablations, downstream evaluation, and compute accounting is easy to follow. Figures have informative captions, and the appendix supplies architecture and optimizer hyperparameters. Ethics: The work presents no evident human-subject, privacy, or direct misuse concern, and it reports hardware and wall-clock costs rather than obscuring the computational burden.
weaknesses: Soundness: The RMS analysis establishes preservation only under strong independence, centering, homoscedasticity, and distributional assumptions that are unlikely to hold exactly for trained Transformer weights and activations. The treatment of SwiGLU gating as a constant-order factor and the extension from linear layers to complete attention/MLP blocks are especially informal. Thus, the theory motivates the method but does not justify the paper's broad RMS-preservation language as an exact guarantee.

There is a concrete limitation in the both-sides-copied derivation for copy ratio c>1: Eq. (37) depends only on c and implicitly assumes uniform replication of every original coordinate. If only some dimensions are copied multiple times, as the text allows, the variance instead depends on the individual replication counts through a sum of squared multiplicities. The stated general formula is therefore not valid without an additional copying assumption.

Evidence: The manuscript reports no independent training repetitions, error bars, or statistical tests. This matters because several final-loss separations are very small and many downstream differences are around one percentage point. Direct measurements of copied-channel divergence, gradient similarity, effective rank, or feature diversity would also support the claimed symmetry-breaking mechanism more convincingly than loss curves alone.

The downstream protocol is underspecified: the paper does not state the shot setting, prompts, decoding/scoring procedure, evaluation harness, or uncertainty. Averaging raw accuracies across heterogeneous tasks further makes the modest aggregate gains difficult to interpret, even though the broad pattern is encouraging.

Generality remains limited. Nearly all evidence uses one OLMoE architecture and scale, one 50%-of-training expansion point, one 2× growth factor, and one pre-training regime; the Muon experiment covers only expert-intermediate expansion. Experiments across expansion times, growth ratios, dense Transformers, and another scale are needed before claiming general width-progressive learning behavior.

Baseline coverage is incomplete. Comparisons focus on naive expansion and selected symmetry-breaking heuristics rather than end-to-end implementations of the strongest recent progressive-width methods discussed in related work. The prior-heuristic tuning budget is also unclear, whereas SPARKLING's re-warmup parameters are explicitly swept.

Reproducibility and limitations: No code, exact training corpus/data order, seeds, channel-copy selection rule, optimizer-state transformation implementation, or evaluation configuration is supplied. There is also an apparent learning-rate inconsistency between Table 4's peak value (1.9556e-3) and Table 5's baseline scaled value (1.449e-3). The limitations discussion is candid about depth expansion and μP, but omits the more immediate restrictions above and does not discuss the environmental cost of the extensive 64-A100 experiments. These issues reduce confidence enough to favor weak accept rather than accept.
